newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Banks wary as EU takes icy look at loan guarantees.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Banks wary as EU takes icy look at loan guarantees.

text.p: Despite strong resistance from EU capitals and banks, the European Commission is considering rules that would make state guarantees for loans and corporate bond issues automatically void if they have not been cleared.
The move, which has been on the cards for more than three years, has so far been successfully countered by European banks, but it is expected to make headway later this year.
"We could be submitting a draft to the member states in the next six months," a Commission official said.

At stake are guarantees attached by national or local authorities to bank loans often granted to ailing businesses which otherwise would get them on less favourable terms or not at all. This is seen as harming fair competition in the European Union.
The new rules would similarly affect corporate bonds issued with a state guarantee, according to the Commission's most recent draft.

The text, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, does not mention unlimited guarantees offered to certain credit institutions themselves, in particular to state-controlled banks such as the German Landesbanken.
But although the Commission is expected to deal with them separately, the new rules are also likely to be of interest for them, said a Brussels-based lawyer well versed in competition rules.

The German savings banks owned by the country's state governments, the most prominent of which is WestLB, have been eyed by the Commission for years because of the unlimited support they receive. This enables them to get maximum credit ratings and to compete with commercial banks.
LOAN GUARANTEES MUST BE SUBMITTED TO COMMISSION

Under existing EU rules, loan guarantees should be submitted to the Commission for clearance before being granted. But such requests are an exception, although EU and industry sources say the number of guarantees granted over the years is huge.
"Guarantees not properly notified to the Commission are illegal as they have been granted in breach of the rules laid down by the Treaty (of the Union)," the draft says.

State guarantees for loans must be cleared by the Commission because they usually amount to a disguised form of subsidy to businesses, which can be allowed only under very strict rules. They contain aid if the interest rate is lower than it would have been without the state intervention.
In the case of a virtually bankrupt company, the state aid involved could equal the entire loan because the company would probably not have obtained credit otherwise.
The banking system is particularly worried about past guarantees, Nicolas Bomcke, secretary-general of the European Banking Federation, told Reuters.
"We expect past guarantees to be honoured," Bomcke said.

This should be the case, according to the text, but only if the terms of the guarantees are brought in line with the new rules -- essentially that they be of a limited duration and do not cover the entirety of a company's debt.

The draft says national governments will have six months from the final publication of the rules to inform the Commission of all existing guarantees granted for commercial activities on non-commercial terms.
But the text warns the banking system that any new guarantees granted without its permission could become void. If ultimately found illegal under EU state aid rules, they could not be honoured.
"The Commission is hardening its position," said Bernard Van de Valle de Ghelcke of the Belgian law firm Boden de Bandt.
Bomcke argued that even if a guarantee was annulled, its issuer should still be responsible and all claims paid.
The Commission also recommended that guarantees should cover only part of a loan not its entirety, implying that banks should take some responsibility for the risk involved.
"This will force the lender to carefully assess the actual credit rating of the borrower," the text said.

The Commission has the power to adopt the rules on its own. However, it is expected to publish a draft text for consultation with the national governments and other interested parties before the adoption of a final position.
